newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel spurns call to quit, defends gold plan.
newsitem.headline: Waigel spurns call to quit, defends gold plan.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Thursday rejected calls to resign over his controversial plan to revalue Germany's gold and currency reserves and insisted the revaluation was a necessary step.

Speaking at a hastily-convened news conference in his home region of Bavaria, Waigel said "not a single mark" of the expected proceeds would go to reduce Germany's budget deficit, which experts say could disqualify Germany from monetary union.
"Germany can meet the EMU criteria even without the reserve revaluation," he told journalists, adding that the move was nonetheless necessary.

Waigel brushed off calls from opposition politicians for his resignation following the Bundesbank's rejection of his plan to book a profit from revaluing the central bank's gold and currency reserves towards market prices.
"I hear calls for my resignation every day. But I have been in office for eight years and I am used to them," he said, adding that he was "very at ease" about his position.

Waigel said the proceeds from the revaluation would flow step by step into a fund created to offset long-term debt, something he said the Bundesbank had in principle accepted as possible from 1999, the planned start-date for EMU.
"What is right in 1999 cannot be wrong in 1997 and 1998," he remarked.
The government plans to transfer part of the gain resulting from the revaluation of Bundesbank gold and currency reserves in several tranche payment starting in 1997 to redeem old debt.
The Bundesbank opposes making the payment before the start of monetary union because it believes such a move would undermine the credibility of the single currency.

German politicians and the press had earlier poured hefty criticism on Waigel and the government for insisting that they would override the respected German central bank and its opposition to the revaluation.
The central bank late on Wednesday issued a statement strongly rejecting Waigel's plan, arguing it ran the risk of damaging confidence in the stability of the new currency, to be called the euro.

One Bundesbank council member, Ernst Welteke, warned Chancellor Helmut Kohl he had failed to win public support for his pet project and that the Bundesbank would command more public sympathy than politicians in a clash.
"Politicians do not have a great deal of credit with the public at the moment," Welteke said in an interview late on Wednesday with German radio.
"The people's trust that the transition period from the deutschemark to the euro can be a stability-oriented one lies much more with the Bundesbank than with politicians," he said.

Financial experts also denounced the grab for gold as a threat to the euro currency Bonn wants to launch on schedule on January 1, 1999 and said Waigel's plan undermined the credibility of the future currency.

"The Bundesbank statement represents a huge slap in the face for Waigel and sets the stage for an open conflict with the government," said Holger Fahrinkrug, an economist at Union Bank of Switzerland in Frankfurt.
German financial markets got a small scare from the clash.
The dollar surged more than a pfennig against the mark in European dealings and German debt prices slumped in London trade since the Frankfurt market was closed for a holiday.
The U.S. currency eased slightly on Waigel's defence of the plan, while Bunds steadied.

Nations seeking to enter European Monetary Union must, among other factors in the Maastricht Treaty, have a 1997 budget deficit of no more than three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and a debt of no more than 60 percent of GDP.
Bonn's deficit figure for 1996 was 3.8 percent and there has been much speculation that it will not be able to qualify for an EMU based on a strict interpretation of the criteria.
The open split with the Bundesbank adds clear domestic political risks to Bonn's troubles.
Kohl has the majority in Bonn to make the necessary law changes to allow the revaluation and opposition politicians attacked his decision to use political power to get his way.
"The government's behaviour endangers what we need most urgently - international credibility," Rudolf Scharping, parliamentary leader of the Social Democrats (SPD) told Thursday's Berliner Zeitung.
He called on Waigel to quit, saying: "The man is no longer tolerable".

Saxony state premier Kurt Biedenkopf, a member of Kohl's Christian Democratic Union (CDU), said Bonn should back down. Going ahead, he said, "means we won't have the authority we need to defend the independence of a European Central Bank".
